## Classification of casualties

Compiling or estimating the numbers of [deaths and wounded](Casualty_(person) "Casualty (person)") caused during wars and other violent conflicts is a [controversial subject](Conflict_epidemiology "Conflict epidemiology"). Historians often put forward many different estimates of the numbers killed and wounded during World War II.[[17]](World_War_II_casualties#cite_note-17) The authors of the *Oxford Companion to World War II* maintain that "casualty statistics are notoriously unreliable".[[18]](World_War_II_casualties#cite_note-18) The table below gives data on the number of dead and military wounded for each country, along with population information to show the relative impact of losses. When scholarly sources differ on the number of deaths in a country, a range of war losses is given, in order to inform readers that the death toll is disputed. Since casualty statistics are sometimes disputed the footnotes to this article present the different estimates by official governmental sources as well as historians. Military figures include [battle deaths](Killed_in_action "Killed in action") (KIA) and [personnel missing in action](Missing_in_action "Missing in action") (MIA), as well as fatalities due to accidents, disease and deaths of prisoners of war in captivity. [Civilian casualties](Civilian_casualties "Civilian casualties") include deaths caused by [strategic bombing](Strategic_bombing_during_World_War_II "Strategic bombing during World War II"), [Holocaust victims](Holocaust_victims "Holocaust victims"), [German war crimes](German_war_crimes#World_War_II "German war crimes"), [Japanese war crimes](Japanese_war_crimes "Japanese war crimes"), [population transfers in the Soviet Union](Population_transfer_in_the_Soviet_Union "Population transfer in the Soviet Union"), [Allied war crimes](Allied_war_crimes_during_World_War_II "Allied war crimes during World War II"), and deaths due to war-related famine and disease.

The sources for the casualties of the individual nations do not use the same methods, and civilian deaths due to starvation and disease make up a large proportion of the civilian deaths in China and the Soviet Union. The losses listed here are actual deaths; hypothetical losses due to a decline in births are not included with the total dead. The distinction between military and civilian casualties caused directly by warfare and [collateral damage](Collateral_damage "Collateral damage") is not always clear-cut. For nations that suffered huge losses such as the Soviet Union, China, Poland, Germany, and Yugoslavia, sources can give only the [total estimated population loss](Demographic_analysis "Demographic analysis") caused by the war and a rough estimate of the breakdown of deaths caused by military activity, [crimes against humanity](Crimes_against_humanity "Crimes against humanity") and war-related famine. The casualties listed here include 19 to 25 million war-related famine deaths in the USSR, China, Indonesia, [Vietnam](Vietnamese_Famine_of_1945 "Vietnamese Famine of 1945"), the Philippines, and [India](Bengal_Famine_of_1943 "Bengal Famine of 1943") that are often omitted from other compilations of World War II casualties.[[19]](World_War_II_casualties#cite_note-ReferenceA-19)[[20]](World_War_II_casualties#cite_note-ReferenceB-20)
